title: Onramp sparklines checklist and demo scripts
content:
Summary:
Small, runnable demo + checklist for onboarding a new engineer or partner to the SDK with an emphasis on the first-5-mins visual: sparklines for latency, tokens/token-cost, and error-rate. Use this during live demos and internal shadowing.

Goals:
- Give a compact sequence that produces a convincing, observable first-run experience (sparklines + logs) in < 10 minutes.
- Surface the minimum telemetry hooks to enable cost/latency sparklines in the console and local dashboards.
- Provide a checklist for common demo flakiness and recovery steps.

Audience:
- Developer advocates running demos
- New SDK integrators in platform teams
- Solutions engineers building quick POCs for customers

Quick notes to self:
- Keep CLI commands deterministic (use --seed 42)
- Use small prompts and short generation lengths to make sparklines readable
- Avoid models with long cold-start times in hosted demo accounts

Demo flows (3 short scripts)
1) Fast hello world (30s)
- Goal: show SDK install, single API call, streaming and sparkline event in dashboard
- Steps:
  1. pip install redwood-sdk==0.8.1  # local env prepped in advance
  2. export REDWOOD_API_KEY=demo-key-xxxx
  3. python -c "from redwood import Client; c=Client(); print(c.generate('Say hi to the world', max_tokens=32))"
  4. open dashboard filter by request-id printed in stdout -> verify latency sparkline and token-bar
- Expected: single short token burst sparkline, status=200, token_cost ~0.0001

2) Chat quickloop (2–3 min)
- Goal: show conversation state, KV cache reuse, and cost delta when caching enabled vs disabled
- Steps:
  1. run local sample chat (examples/chat_fastloop.py) with --cache on then off
  2. emit two consecutive similar prompts and observe token consumption sparklines side-by-side
- CLI example: python examples/chat_fastloop.py --seed 42 --cache on --count 2
- Notes: show developer console toggle for prefix caching; point out 'cache hit' metric in timeline

3) Failure mode + graceful fallback (3–5 min)
- Goal: demonstrate model fallback policy and its impact on latency/cost sparklines
- Steps:
  1. Configure runner with primary=model-x-small fallback=model-x-tiny (demo config file included)
  2. Inject artificial capacity constraint via local proxy (scripts/fail_primary.sh)
  3. Trigger 10 concurrent requests and show automatic fallback - latency spike then stable lower-cost fallback
- Observables: request shards showing policy decision, cost per-token transition in sparkline

Required telemetry hooks (minimal)
- request_id (uuid) emitted to stdout and console
- model_name, model_variant
- latency_ms (client-observed) per request and per token (if streaming)
- tokens_consumed, input_tokens, output_tokens
- cache_hit boolean for KV/prefix cache flows
- error_code / http_status

Sparklines to surface in first-run UI (priority order)
- latency_ms (1s resolution)  — show moving sparkline for last 60s
- tokens_per_request (bar-spark) — quick visual of cost impact per call
- success_rate / error_rate (percent) — small area graph updated per minute
- fallback_events (tick marks) — small annotation layer on latency sparkline

Checklist (pre-demo)
- [ ] Demo account has valid API key and usage quota
- [ ] Demo runner configured to use small models (low cost)
- [ ] Local environment: python 3.11, latest pip, venv activated
- [ ] Terminal visibility: make sure dashboard and terminal are side-by-side on the projector
- [ ] Noise budget: enable streaming throttles to avoid long outputs

Checklist (during demo)
- [ ] Print request_id for each run and point to it in dashboard
- [ ] Point out the token bar and explain per-token cost briefly
- [ ] Toggle cache on/off to show cost delta (if time)
- [ ] If fallback triggers, explain policy and expected behavior

Post-demo checklist
- [ ] Save request_ids to GH issue / demo notes for reproducibility
- [ ] Capture screenshot of sparklines and attach to PR / Confluence
- [ ] Log any confusing UX notes for engineers (where sparklines were misleading)

Runbook snippets (copy/paste)
- print request id from Python client:
  from redwood import Client
  c = Client()
  r = c.generate('smol test', max_tokens=16)
  print('request_id:', r.request_id)

- replay a request on the console (curl):
  curl -H "Authorization: Bearer demo-key-xxxx" -d '{"prompt":"replay test","max_tokens":16}' https://api.redwood.ai/v1/generate

Troubleshooting (common demo flakiness)
- No events in dashboard: confirm API key scope includes telemetry:read and demo account retention window
- Streaming stalls: check network (throttling) and model cold-start; recommend pre-warm with a 1-token request 30s before demo
- Token counts off vs console: ensure client version matches server-side schema for token accounting (see linked PR)

Open questions / follow-ups:
- Do we want a one-click pre-warm option in the console for demo accounts? (ux-rfc pending)
- Should sparklines include per-route cost breakdown (vs global) — UX wants this but cost backend changes needed
- Can we generate a synthetic 'demo mode' dataset so advocates don't burn real credits? (ticket: DEMO-72)

Short-term todos (next week)
- [ ] Publish example repo with three demo scripts (fast-hello, chat-quickloop, failover) — assigned to Riley
- [ ] Add request_id printing to all example apps — assigned to Priya
- [ ] Draft one-pager for sales with sparkline screenshots and callouts — assigned to Ethan

References / links:
- GitHub PR w/ token schema changes: https://github.com/redwood-inference/sdk/pull/987
- Example chat script: examples/chat_fastloop.py (repo root)
- Slack thread: #devx-demo-scripts (pinned messages)

Notes-to-self (informal):
- Don't over-explain token math in public demos — show relative cost instead
- Keep sample prompts non-sensitive and short; use "weather summary" or "tiny story"
- We should add a dedicated demo key with limited quota and pre-warm endpoint next quarter
